cues.text: Hey, welcome back.
Optical experiments begin with finding an image, not just writing an equation.
On an optical bench, align a concave mirror and a bright object pin at the
same
height.
Find its real inverted image, then use an image pin to locate that image
accurately.
Move your eye slightly sideways.
If the image tip and image pin tip slide relative to each other, they are at
different depths.
Adjust the image pin until that relative motion disappears.
That is removing parallax.
Merely making two tips overlap from one viewing position is not enough.
Measure object and image positions relative to the mirror's pole, applying any
measured bench correction.
Choose the incident light direction as positive.
For a real object and a real image in front of this mirror, u and v are both
negative.
Our original example has u equal
to minus twenty four centimeters and v equal to minus forty eight centimeters.
The mirror equation gives one over f equals minus one over twenty four minus
one over forty eight, or minus one over sixteen.
Therefore f is minus sixteen centimeters.
The negative sign identifies the focus in front of the mirror under this
convention.
Repeat for several suitable object positions and compare the results.
A sharply formed distant object image gives an approximate starting focal
length, but its object distance is not literally infinite.
Never view the Sun through optical equipment or deliberately focus sunlight
for
this exercise.
Use safe illumination, careful alignment and paraxial rays.
For a thin convex lens in air, light travels from left to right.
A real object is on the left, so u is negative.
Its real transmitted image is on the right, so v is positive.
The lens equation is one over f equals one over v minus one over u.
Notice that this is not the mirror equation.
Suppose the corrected measurements are u equal to minus thirty centimeters and
v equal to plus sixty centimeters.
One over f is one over sixty plus one over thirty, giving f equal to plus
twenty centimeters.
Positive f is consistent with a converging lens in air.
An image pin is positioned where its tip and the image tip show no relative
movement as you move your eye sideways.
Keep the principal axis horizontal and the tips at the optical center's
height.
Now let capital U and V mean positive magnitudes of the real object and image
distances.
Then one over f equals one over U plus one over V.
If x is one over U and y is one over V, the graph is y equals minus x plus one
over f.
Its intercept is one over f and its slope is minus one.
If the intercept is zero point zero five inverse centimeters, f is twenty
centimeters.
That intercept is not twenty itself.
Use multiple corrected readings and fit the trend rather than forcing every
observation onto a perfect line.
Lens thickness, misalignment and measurement uncertainty limit the thin lens
approximation.
A concave lens with a real object normally produces a virtual image that
cannot
be caught on a screen.
So how can an optical bench measure its focal length using real images?
First use a convex lens to form a real image and locate that position
carefully.
Keep the object and convex lens fixed.
Insert the concave lens between the convex lens and that original image
position.
The incident rays are already converging.
Their would be meeting point lies to the right of the concave lens, making it
a
virtual object for that lens.
Therefore u is positive.
The concave lens reduces the convergence; if the original meeting point is
sufficiently close, the rays still meet farther to the right.
Locate the new real image by removing parallax with an image pin.
In our example, the original focus is twelve centimeters to the right of the
inserted concave lens, while the final image is thirty centimeters to its
right.
Thus u is plus twelve and v is plus thirty.
One over f equals one over thirty minus one over twelve, giving f equal to
minus twenty centimeters.
The sign correctly identifies a diverging lens.
Here twelve is less than the focal length magnitude twenty, which allows the
final real image.
If u equals that magnitude, the outgoing beam is parallel in the ideal model.
If u is larger, the outgoing rays diverge and this real image measurement no
longer works.
Do not replace u with the original object's distance from the convex lens.
Every distance in this calculation belongs to the inserted concave lens.
A prism changes a ray's direction at two surfaces.
Measure incidence i and emergence e from the respective surface normals, and
let A be the prism angle.
The total deviation is i plus e minus A.
Trace several paths using a narrow safe light source or carefully aligned
pins,
record the angles, and plot deviation against incidence.
Deviation first falls and then rises.
The lowest point is the minimum deviation, D m, not simply the first value in
your table.
At this symmetric path, i equals e and the two internal refraction angles are
each A divided by two.
Applying Snell's law gives the prism's refractive index relative to air: sine
of half the sum of A and D m, divided by sine of half A.
Our original example has a sixty degree prism and minimum deviation forty
degrees.
The numerator is sine fifty degrees, and the denominator is sine thirty
degrees.
Their ratio is about one point five three two.
At minimum, the incidence and emergence angles are both fifty degrees,
consistent with delta equal to fifty plus fifty minus sixty.
A measured deviation of forty degrees is useful in this formula only when it
is
the minimum.
Keep the prism outline fixed while tracing each path, draw normals rather than
measuring from a face, and use the correct angle units on your calculator.
Repeated observations near the turning point improve the estimate.
Do not stare into a beam or use sunlight for alignment.
A mark beneath a transparent slab appears closer to the top surface than it
really is.
For near normal viewing from air, refractive index is real depth divided by
apparent depth.
A travelling microscope lets us measure the two depths using focus positions.
First focus a bottom reference mark without the slab and record its vertical
reading.
Then place the slab over the mark and focus the mark's raised image through
the slab.
Finally focus a small visible reference on the slab's top surface.
In our original example, the corrected focus coordinates increase upward:
bottom mark at one centimeter, apparent image at two centimeters, and top
surface at four centimeters.
The real thickness is four minus one, or three centimeters.
The apparent thickness is four minus two, or two centimeters.
Refractive index is three divided by two, giving one point five.
The apparent rise is one centimeter; it is not the apparent thickness.
If your microscope scale increases downward instead, use the appropriate
positive differences rather than blindly keeping our subtraction order.
Approach the final focus from a consistent direction to reduce backlash,
determine the scale's least count, and repeat the readings.
A constant coordinate zero cancels in a difference, but calibration and
focusing errors do not necessarily cancel.
These equations assume a uniform parallel sided slab, air outside, and small
viewing angles.
Our examples illustrate inference from measurements; they are not claimed
observations or official past paper questions.
In JEE, define the reference position before trusting a numerical answer.
